They had to remove 14 days of impacted stool by hand at the ER.

If you're chronically constipated, please read this before you end up like me.

I hadn't gone to the bathroom in 14 days.

I told my husband I was fine.

I took another Miralax, then a Senna, then two Dulcolax, and washed it all down with a bottle of magnesium citrate the size of a small soda.

Nothing.

By day 15, I was doubled over on the bathroom floor, unable to stand up from the pressure in my abdomen.

That's when my husband Robert picked me up off the cold tile, carried me to our SUV in nothing but a robe, and drove me to the ER at 2:47 in the morning.

What the doctor said next, about WHY my bowels had stopped working completely, changed everything I thought I knew about my body.

And it's the reason I'm writing this post tonight.

Because if you're a woman over 45 who has been silently struggling with constipation, straining, bloating, or that backed up and heavy feeling like there's still something inside you at the end of every day…

Please read this all the way through.

What I'm about to share with you is the same information that turned my life around in 4 weeks, and it could save yours too.

My name is Margaret. I'm 52 years old. I live in suburban Pennsylvania with my husband Robert.

And like a lot of women my age, I've been quietly battling a constipation problem for years.

It started in my early 40s, around the time I went into perimenopause. Just little things at first. Going every other day instead of every day. Some bloating after dinner. A little discomfort.

But by 47, I was barely going twice a week.

By 49, I was on Miralax every single morning just to function.

And by 51, I was doing everything you can imagine to get my bowels to move.

I had tried EVERYTHING. All the laxatives. The teas. The prune juice. A gallon of water a day. 30 grams of fiber. Digestive enzymes. Probiotics. You name it, I'd taken it.

Nothing was working.

I had two gastroenterologists tell me I had "IBS-C" and to "just keep taking the Miralax."

A third told me my colon was "redundant" and "kinked" and there was nothing to be done.

A fourth ordered a colonoscopy that came back completely normal.

And in the meantime, I was getting worse.

I felt backed up and heavy all the time, like there was something sitting inside me that would not come out no matter what I did. My lower stomach was hard and swollen by the afternoon, and I couldn't take a proper deep breath after dinner.

The brain fog had gotten so bad I'd forget words mid sentence. I had a constant low grade headache that no one could explain.

I was waking up at 3am with this terrible, gripping anxiety I'd never had before in my life. My joints ached, my energy was gone, and my mood was in the toilet.

I had become a stranger in my own body.

And then came the night that nearly killed me.

It started on a Tuesday. By Friday I realized I hadn't gone since the previous Wednesday. That's 9 days.

I doubled my Miralax. Took a Senna. Drank a quart of warm prune juice.

Saturday morning, still nothing.

Sunday, I added Dulcolax to the mix. I felt some movement, so I sat on the toilet for 45 minutes straining, and a few small hard pellets came out. I told myself I was going.

I wasn't.

By Tuesday of the next week, I was on day 14. My stomach was so distended I couldn't button any of my pants. I felt like I had a bowling ball lodged behind my ribs, and I couldn't take a deep breath without sharp pain.

But I told Robert I was fine.

Because I was so used to suffering through this in silence, I'd lost the ability to admit how bad it had gotten.

Around 2 in the morning, I tried to get out of bed to go to the bathroom and just collapsed.

Robert woke up to me on the floor, pale, sweating, unable to speak. He didn't ask. He just picked me up, wrapped me in a robe, and carried me to the car.

By 3:15am we were in the ER at our local hospital.

By 4am I was on a stretcher, hooked up to an IV, getting wheeled in for an emergency CT scan.

And by 5:30am, the ER doctor, a woman about my age named Dr. Sarah Chen, came to my bed with the scan results in her hand.

She sat down on the edge of the bed and gently told me what they'd found.

I had 14 days of impacted stool packed into my colon. It was so dried out and compacted that no laxative was going to move it. Not anymore.

They were going to have to remove it manually, right there in the hospital.

I couldn't even look at her.

I'm not going to describe what happened next, because it's the most humiliating experience of my life.

But by 8am that morning, the impaction was out. I was exhausted, sore, embarrassed, and I just wanted to go home and never speak of it again.

But before I could leave, Dr. Chen came back into the room.

She pulled up a chair next to my bed, looked me in the eye, and said something I wasn't expecting at all.

"Mrs. Whitman, before you go home, I need you to understand something. The stool we just removed isn't your problem. It's the symptom. There's a reason you've been struggling with constipation for years that no one has ever told you about. And unless you address it, this is going to keep happening for the rest of your life."

I just stared at her.

For the first time in 6 years, a doctor was about to actually explain what was wrong with me.

Dr. Chen took a breath and started from the beginning.

She told me what I had wasn't really "IBS-C." It wasn't a "redundant colon." It wasn't "just menopause."

She said the real problem was much simpler than that.

👉 "Mrs. Whitman, your colon is dry."

I told her that was impossible. I drank more water than anyone I knew, a gallon a day, sometimes more.

She nodded like she'd heard it a thousand times before.

👉 "I believe you, and I'm sure it barely helped, because almost none of that water ever reaches the part of you that needs it. The water you drink gets absorbed high up, in your small intestine and the first stretch of your colon, and from there it goes straight into your bloodstream."

"By the time anything gets down to the far end where your stool is actually sitting and waiting, there's very little left."

I asked her why that mattered so much.

That's when she explained the part that made my jaw drop.

👉 "Because a soft, easy bowel movement is basically water. A healthy stool is around 75% water, and that is the entire difference between one that slides out on its own and one that sits there hard and dry and stuck."

"It has almost nothing to do with fiber, and far less to do with how much you drink than anyone ever told you. What matters is whether the water actually arrives where the stool is."

"Your colon is supposed to be a wet place. When it's wet, everything moves. When it dries out, everything in it stops."

She paused for a second, then went on.

👉 "And your colon wall doesn't just sit quietly while that happens. Its whole job is to suck water out of anything passing through it. That's completely normal, it's what it was built to do."

"But right now it's sucking water out of a stool that has nothing coming in to replace it."

"So every hour that stool sits inside you, it gets drier and harder and more compacted, until eventually it can't move at all."

"That's why it hurts when you go. That's why you're passing small hard pieces instead of anything normal. And it's why you never feel empty."

I felt sick.

It was finally starting to make sense, but I still didn't understand why my body had let this happen in the first place.

Dr. Chen leaned in for the next part.

👉 "Because your gut is supposed to be actively pulling water into your colon and flooding it, so that whatever is sitting there stays soft and keeps moving. That's a real job your body does every single day without you ever thinking about it."

"And the mineral that runs that job is magnesium. Magnesium is what tells your gut to pull the water in."

Then she told me what happens to that mineral after we hit 50.

👉 "Three things go after your magnesium at the same time."

"The food supply carries far less of it than it did a generation ago, so the same vegetables your mother ate don't give you anything close to what they gave her."

"Your gut absorbs less of what you do eat, which is just part of getting older."

"And the everyday medications sitting on your bathroom shelf actively strip it out of you, particularly acid reducers and blood pressure pills, along with most of the other chronic medications people your age take every single day."

I sat there in that hospital gown doing the math.

I was on two of the three.

But she still wasn't finished, and the last piece was the one that finally explained why nothing had ever held for me.

👉 "Even when water does make it down to your colon, it doesn't stay inside the stool. It sits loose around it instead, and your colon wall sucks it right back out again."

"So on the rare occasion something finally works, you're dry all over again by the next day."

"You have two problems happening at once, Mrs. Whitman. Not enough water is reaching your colon, and what does reach it doesn't stay in the poop."

I sat there as a 52 year old woman in a hospital gown, hearing the explanation for everything that had been wrong with me for years.

But Dr. Chen wasn't done.

👉 "And while all of that is sitting cemented inside you for days at a time, you're carrying waste that should have left your body a week ago."

"That's where the bloating comes from, and the pressure behind your ribs, and the exhaustion. It's where the brain fog comes from, the 3am anxiety, and that low grade headache you've been putting down to just being 52."

"None of it is aging. Your colon has gone dry, and your body is holding onto two weeks of waste it was never built to hold."

I sat there in that hospital bed in complete silence.

Because every single one of my doctors had missed it.

Six years of being told it was IBS-C. Six years of being told to just take more Miralax. Six years of being told to drink more water and eat more fiber, when more water was never going to reach the problem and more fiber was quietly making it worse.

And the whole time, the answer had been sitting right there.

I asked Dr. Chen the obvious question. "So how do I fix this?"

She told me there IS a way, but it's not what I'd been doing for the last 6 years, and it's simpler than anything my gastroenterologists ever suggested.

Not drink more water.

Not eat more fiber.

Not another laxative.

She said that to actually solve the root cause of my constipation, three things had to happen, in this exact order:

✅ First, I had to get water back into the dry colon.

Not more water in my mouth, but water pulled directly into the colon itself, down where the stool is actually sitting. Until that whole environment was wet again, nothing else I did was going to matter.

✅ Second, that water had to get pulled INSIDE the stool and stay there.

Not sitting loose in the colon where the wall sucks it straight back out. Inside the stool, held there, so it stays soft the entire way down.

✅ Third, whatever moved it had to work with my colon instead of forcing it.

This was the one she stressed the most. Stimulant laxatives whip the colon into contracting, and that's where the cramping and the pain come from.

It's also where the dependency comes from, because your gut stops doing the work on its own and you need a stronger dose every year just to keep up.

Then she walked me through why every single thing I'd been doing had failed.

👉 "Drinking more water fails the first step, because it's absorbed long before it ever gets down there."

👉 "Fiber fails the first two. All it does is add dry bulk to a stool that has no water in it, so you end up with something bigger and drier than what you started with, and the gas on top of it."

👉 "Stimulant laxatives fail all three. They force the plug out once and never put back a single drop of water, which is exactly why it hurts so much and why you needed a stronger one every year."

I told her I'd stop at the drugstore on the way home and grab a bigger bottle of magnesium.

🛑 "You're close," she said. "But the form matters more than the size of the bottle."

👉 "What you want is magnesium oxide. It's an oxidised form, which means it isn't built to be absorbed into your bloodstream the way the ones marketed for sleep and muscle cramps are."

"It stays down in the gut, right where the stool actually is, and it draws water into the colon there. That makes it the best one for hydrating a dry colon naturally, and it's gentle about it. There's nothing harsh going on."

"Then you need something that pulls that water inside the stool and holds it there, or your colon wall takes it straight back and you're dry again by tomorrow. That's kiwifruit."

She explained that kiwifruit fiber binds water directly into the stool itself and holds onto it, so the water the magnesium just brought in gets trapped where you actually need it rather than sitting loose around it.

The colon wall can't suck it back out. The stool stays soft the whole way down.

And unlike the fiber that had been making me worse for years, it does this without fermenting into gas.

"Then there's one last piece that helps your colon carry it out. It's a fruit and berry blend called triphala."

"It gently tones and strengthens the muscle so it can do its job on its own. It doesn't force anything, and it doesn't whip your colon into contracting, so there's no cramping and nothing for your gut to become dependent on."

She told me she'd been recommending this combination to her patients for years.

Most of them had gone from exactly where I was, backed up for days at a time and terrified of the pain, to going every single morning on their own.

I asked her whether they were taking any particular brand.

👉 "You can buy all three separately," she said. "Plenty of women do, and it works fine."

"But quite a few of my patients have moved onto one called Regularity Reset, because it puts all three into one capsule at the right doses. You're not standing in your kitchen every night trying to measure out three different things."

She wrote the name down on a hospital pad and slid it across the bed.

Then she told me what was actually in it:

500mg of magnesium oxide, the form that stays down in the gut and floods your dry colon with water instead of disappearing into your bloodstream

500mg of kiwifruit extract, to pull that water inside the stool and hold it there so your colon wall can't suck it back out, without the gas

300mg of triphala extract, to tone and strengthen the muscle so it carries everything out on its own, with no forcing and no cramping

"Magnesium puts the water back into the colon. Kiwifruit pulls it inside the stool and keeps it there. Triphala helps your colon move it out."

"That's the three step process magnesium alone never had, and it's exactly why this time it doesn't quit on you after a day."

"It's a small family run business and they only sell it on their own website. Fair warning though, they run out of stock fairly often, so check before you get your hopes up."

That morning, after I'd been disimpacted and discharged, Robert drove me home at 9am.

I didn't even change out of the hospital clothes. I sat down at the kitchen table, pulled up the website on my phone, and ordered a bottle of Regularity Reset right then and there.

It arrived three days later.

I took my first dose that night. Three capsules with a glass of water, right before bed.

Here's exactly what happened over the next four weeks.

✅ Week 1

I took three capsules every night before bed. No cramping. No sudden urgency in the middle of the night. Nothing that had me watching the clock.

By the fourth morning, I had my first complete bowel movement in years, without a laxative.

And it was soft. I didn't strain, I didn't brace myself, I didn't grab onto anything. It simply came out.

I sat there for a long time afterwards just trying to take it in. Robert knocked on the door to check on me. All I could tell him was that I'd gone.

✅ Week 2

I went every single morning, like clockwork.

That heavy, backed up feeling I'd been carrying around for years was more than half gone, and for the first time in ages my pants buttoned all the way up at 8pm.

I could feel the brain fog starting to lift too. I was sharper and quicker, more like the woman I used to be at 40.

✅ Week 3

The 3am anxiety stopped. I slept through the night for 7 nights in a row, which I genuinely couldn't remember doing in years.

The constant low grade headache I'd had for the last 4 years was gone. My joints stopped aching, and my energy came roaring back.

And I stopped thinking about it, which sounds like a small thing but isn't. For six years, my very first thought every morning was whether today was going to be a bad day.

That thought just stopped showing up.

✅ Week 4

Dr. Chen had given me her office number before I left the hospital and asked me to call and let her know how I got on.

So I called her.

I told her I was going every morning, on my own, with no laxatives at all. That nothing hurt. That my stomach was soft again.

She was quiet for a second, and then she said: "That's exactly what I hoped I'd hear, Mrs. Whitman."

I wasn't constipated anymore. I wasn't bloated anymore. I wasn't foggy anymore.

I felt 30 years old again.

How can a 58-year-old woman spend SIX HOURS passing what looked like a month’s worth of stool when she had been “pooping” every few days?

That was the question running through my head at 1:17 in the morning, the night before my colonoscopy.

The bowel prep had done absolutely nothing for nearly two hours.

Then a piece of stool so large and hard came out that I screamed.

And once it moved...

Everything behind it started coming.

Load after load after load.

Every time I thought I was finished, another wave hit.

By the fourth trip, I was shaking.

By the tenth, I was staring into the toilet thinking:

Where the hell had all of this been hiding?

I hadn’t eaten solid food all day.

And I had supposedly been “going” every three or four days.

So why did it look like my body had been holding onto weeks of waste?

The next morning, my gastroenterologist asked me one question that made my stomach drop:

“When was the last time you had a complete bowel movement without Miralax, Senna or Dulcolax?”

I opened my mouth to answer.

And realized I couldn’t remember.

I was 58 years old.

I had been constipated for more than four years.

It started when menopause hit in my early fifties.

And until that morning, I genuinely believed that dropping three or four rabbit pellets into the toilet every few days meant I was still going.

I was wrong.

And what Dr. Harper explained after my colonoscopy finally made the previous four years make sense:

Why I could drink water all day and still pass dry rocks...

Why fiber made my stomach feel even bigger...

Why Miralax gave me results I could never predict...

And why the strongest laxatives only restarted the same miserable cycle.

Before menopause, I had always been regular.

I would have my coffee in the morning, use the bathroom and get on with my day.

I barely thought about it.

Then menopause came and my body seemed to change all at once.

The hot flashes started.

My sleep became terrible.

My waist thickened even though I wasn’t eating differently.

And my digestion slowed to a crawl.

At first, I would skip one day.

Then two.

Eventually, I could go four or five days without what I would now call a proper bowel movement.

But I didn’t tell anyone.

I was embarrassed.

Even with my husband, I would quietly take something and hope he didn’t notice how often I disappeared into the bathroom.

I had Miralax in the kitchen cupboard.

Senna beside my bed.

Dulcolax in my handbag.

Fiber gummies in the car.

And a bottle of magnesium citrate hidden behind the towels for what I called “real emergencies.”

My husband called it Linda’s pharmacy.

I laughed whenever he said it.

But privately, I was scared.

Without something from that collection, my body barely did anything.

And when I finally did go, it was rarely normal.

Usually, three or four hard little pellets would drop into the toilet.

Sometimes they were so dry they left absolutely nothing on the paper.

Other times, one large piece would become stuck halfway out.

I would sit there rocking, sweating and pushing until my legs went numb.

Then I would stand up and still feel as if most of it was sitting inside me.

But I always told myself the same thing:

“At least something came out.”

That was how I convinced myself I wasn’t really constipated.

Then last spring, my doctor mailed me one of those at-home colon screening tests.

I left it sitting on the bathroom counter for almost a month.

Partly because nobody enjoys collecting a stool sample.

But mostly because I kept waiting until I had enough of a bowel movement to complete it.

When I finally did, the result came back abnormal.

Blood had been detected.

My doctor said it could be hemorrhoids.

But naturally, my mind went straight to something worse.

Within ten minutes of putting down the phone, I had convinced myself I had colon cancer.

She referred me for a colonoscopy.

The appointment was five weeks away.

Those five weeks were horrible.

Every ache frightened me.

Every time I saw blood on the toilet paper, my stomach dropped.

My daughter eventually made me promise I would stop searching my symptoms online because I had diagnosed myself with six different diseases.

By the time the procedure arrived, I just wanted an answer.

The day before my colonoscopy, I followed the preparation instructions exactly.

I stopped eating solid food.

I had broth, lemon gelatin and clear liquids.

At six that evening, I mixed the bowel preparation and drank the first portion.

Everyone had warned me to stay near the bathroom.

So I waited.

An hour passed.

Nothing.

Then another half hour.

Still nothing.

My stomach was bubbling and making awful noises.

I could feel liquid moving around inside me.

But I couldn’t go.

I started panicking that I was going to fail the preparation and they would cancel my procedure.

Then I felt an enormous amount of pressure low down.

I rushed to the bathroom.

What came out first was not liquid.

It was one large, painfully hard piece of stool.

It felt like trying to pass a stone.

I gripped the edge of the sink and breathed through it.

At one point, I genuinely thought I might have to wake my husband and ask him to take me to the hospital.

But then it finally moved.

The relief lasted about thirty seconds.

Because once that hard piece came out...

Everything behind it started coming.

For the next six hours, I went back and forth to the bathroom more times than I could count.

At first, there was an unbelievable amount of solid stool.

Every time I thought I had finished, another wave hit.

Then it became loose.

Then watery.

By the middle of the night, I was passing pale yellow liquid.

I was exhausted.

My legs felt weak.

My backside was sore.

But for the first time in years, my lower stomach didn’t feel hard and heavy.

I felt empty.

Actually empty.

My daughter drove me to the endoscopy center the next morning.

A nurse checked me in and asked whether I had completed the entire preparation.

I told her yes.

Then she asked what my final bowel movements looked like.

I said they were pale yellow and almost clear.

She nodded and said that was exactly what they wanted.

They put an IV in my hand.

The anesthesiologist told me to take a deep breath.

And then everything went dark.

The next thing I remember was hearing my name.

My daughter was sitting beside the bed when I opened my eyes.

A few minutes later, the gastroenterologist came through the curtain.

Her name was Dr. Melissa Harper.

She told me the colonoscopy had gone well.

There was no tumor.

There was no blockage.

She had found small internal hemorrhoids, which likely explained the bright red blood, but nothing dangerous.

The relief that went through me was indescribable.

I immediately started crying.

My daughter started crying too.

Dr. Harper waited for both of us to calm down.

Then she pulled over a chair.

She said the colonoscopy looked reassuring.

But something on my intake form concerned her.

Under “bowel movement frequency,” I had written:

“One or two times a week, usually with laxatives.”

She asked how long that had been happening.

I told her more than four years.

Then she asked what my bowel movements normally looked like.

I told her about the pellets.

The straining.

The hard pieces that felt stuck.

The constant pressure.

And how I almost never felt completely empty afterward.

Then I told her what had happened during the preparation.

How nothing happened at first.

How that first hard piece felt like a plug.

And how an unbelievable amount came out after it moved.

Dr. Harper looked at me and said:

“Linda, you have severe chronic constipation.”

I felt embarrassed hearing her say it so plainly.

I told her I thought I was still going because something came out every few days.

She shook her head.

“Passing a few dry pellets is not the same as having a complete bowel movement,” she said.

“Those pellets are one of the clearest signs that your stool has been sitting inside you too long.”

The colon naturally absorbs water.

But when stool moves through too slowly, it remains inside the colon longer.

And the longer it sits there, the more moisture gets pulled out of it.

Stool that may have been soft enough to pass on the first or second day becomes progressively drier by the fourth or fifth day.

Then the dry stool becomes even harder to move.

Because it cannot move properly, it stays inside longer.

And while it sits there, still more water is removed.

The stool moves slowly.

It loses moisture.

It becomes hard.

Then the hard stool moves even more slowly.

Those little dry pieces weren’t evidence that everything was working.

They were evidence that my stool had lost too much moisture before it came out.

The prep had brought a large amount of fluid into my bowel.

Once that piece passed, everything behind it could finally move through.

Miralax.

Senna.

Dulcolax.

Fiber gummies.

Prune juice.

Magnesium citrate when I became desperate.

Being completely backed up...

Magnesium oxide

It helps draw water into the intestinal tract so the stool has enough moisture to soften.

Kiwifruit extract

The stool needed to absorb that water and hold onto it. Otherwise, it could start drying out again as it moved through the colon.

The concentrated kiwifruit extract helped the stool retain that moisture so it could become soft, stay soft and pass more easily.

Triphala

Because even softened stool still has to move before it begins drying out again.
